name: Under-eye filler (tear trough)

card.summary: Filler placed in the hollow under the eyes to soften shadowing; widely used and fairly well described, but a high-skill area where delayed swelling, lumps and rare vision-threatening events are documented.
card.note: Swelling after treatment is common; delayed lumps and rare orbital and vascular complications are reported in the literature.

quick.overview:
Tear trough filler is the injection of a soft gel, usually hyaluronic acid, into the groove between the lower eyelid and the cheek to reduce hollowing and dark shadows. It is used by clinicians as a non-surgical alternative to lower eyelid surgery.

On looksmaxxing forums it is mentioned as a small adjustment that can be noticeable in person without a plastic look. Medical literature describes it as common but technically demanding, with no standard evidence-based technique.
quick.mechanism: Filler placed in the tear trough camouflages the hollow and the bulge of orbital fat that creates a shadow, by adding volume under the skin [1]. HA was the most commonly reported product in delayed-complication cases, with poly-L-lactic acid and calcium hydroxylapatite also reported [2].
quick.risks: Swelling after infraorbital HA filler occurred in over half of patients in one retrospective review of 706 treatments, and was lower when a small amount of triamcinolone was mixed with the filler [4]. A systematic review of delayed complications identified swelling, lumps and xanthelasma-like reactions [2]. A first case of orbital compartment syndrome with retrobulbar haemorrhage after tear trough filler has been reported, managed without lasting visual loss [5].

lead: Under-eye filler, usually called tear trough filler, is the injection of a soft gel, most often hyaluronic acid (HA), into the groove that runs from the inner corner of the eye down toward the cheek. The aim is to fill the hollow so the lower eyelid blends into the cheek, which softens the shadow that makes the eyes look tired, sunken or dark [1][3]. Reviews describe fillers as able to camouflage both the tear trough deformity and the look of bulging orbital fat, because added volume under the skin evens out the contour [1].

In looksmaxxing communities the procedure is discussed as a small, targeted adjustment to the eye area, which is central to how a face reads in person. Forum posters describe it as an in-clinic procedure with a quick recovery, and they compare it with fat grafting as a way of treating hollow under-eyes [16][17][12]. Clinicians present it as a non-surgical alternative to lower eyelid surgery for people with hollowing but without much excess skin [8][18].

The published research is mostly retrospective: one systematic review of 42 articles on HA tear trough techniques found most of the evidence to be level III and no standardised technique [3], while a consecutive series of 198 eyes in 100 patients tracked satisfaction after HA treatment [8]. Documented problems include post-injection swelling, delayed lumps and discolouration, and rare vascular and orbital events [4][2][5]. In the United States fillers are regulated as medical devices, and the FDA's consumer page does not list the under-eye area among approved uses [14].

chain: Gel is placed in the hollow between the lower eyelid and cheek
Volume fills the groove and softens the shadow cast by the lid-cheek step
Eyes look less hollow and tired, usually within days once swelling settles
angle.text: People use under-eye filler to make the lower eyelid blend into the cheek, which reduces the dark, hollow look under the eyes. The effect is temporary with HA, so users describe it as something that is maintained or repeated rather than a one-off change.

paras: The tear trough is the depression running from the medial canthus toward the cheek. In the periorbital region, neuromodulators lift the brow and soften lines, whereas fillers are used to camouflage the tear trough and the look of orbital fat pseudoherniation [1]. Two features tend to create the tired-eye look: the hollow itself and the bulge of fat above it, and filler treats both by adding volume at the step between them [1].

Two delivery tools are used. A sharp needle places filler at depth in small amounts, and a blunt cannula slides along pre-planned paths. A series of 1,452 tear trough applications between 2016 and 2020 described a cannula method that uses tailored linear paths and a three-point tangent approach [7]. A systematic review that looked for a difference between needle and cannula found no significant difference in reported aesthetic results and no standardised, evidence-based technique [3].

Lower eyelid blepharoplasty is the surgical counterpart. Wikipedia describes it as addressing fat protrusion, skin laxity and the eyelid-cheek contour, with fat repositioned along the infraorbital rim or autologous fat transferred to restore volume [15]. Reviews of lower blepharoplasty state that the transconjunctival route, with an incision inside the lid, suits younger patients with prominent fat herniation and no excess skin, while the transcutaneous route is used where skin laxity is present [18]. The term blepharoplasty itself dates to 1818, when Karl Ferdinand von Graefe used it for eyelid repair, according to Wikipedia [15].

Other injectables have been studied for the same hollow. Registered or published studies include platelet-rich fibrin for tear trough rejuvenation [9], a combination of two HA fillers [10], an extracellular matrix and stromal vascular fraction gel [19], autologous cultured fibroblasts for the nasojugal groove [20] and a composite collagen-crosslinked HA filler [21]. Forum users also discuss fat grafting as an alternative and compare it with filler [16][17].

Evidence on appearance outcomes is mainly retrospective and non-experimental. Most of the 42 articles in the HA technique review were level III [3]. In a consecutive case series of 198 eyes in 100 patients, mostly white women, one surgeon treated the tear trough with an HA gel over 18 months and assessed outcomes with masked photograph grading and a satisfaction survey, with an average follow-up of 5.1 months [8].

Registered trials show where the research is going. NCT04577898 compared the HA product RHA Redensity Eye with no treatment for infraorbital hollows in 248 participants [11]. NCT00852241 was a pilot of two HA fillers in the lower eyelid in 18 participants [10], NCT05694286 was a small prospective evaluation of infraorbital filler injection in 11 participants [22], and NCT05647551 followed satisfaction with the periorbital area after filler and neuromodulator injections in 73 adults [23]. A multicentre safety evaluation of a semi-cross-linked HA filler for tear trough rejuvenation has also been published [24].

The FDA's consumer page lists bruising, redness, swelling, pain, tenderness, itching and rash as common effects of dermal fillers generally [14]. In a retrospective review of 447 patients and 706 infraorbital HA treatments, swelling occurred in 51 percent of patients not given triamcinolone and in 23 percent when a low dose of triamcinolone was mixed into the filler; swelling rose with the volume injected [4].

A systematic review of 52 published cases of delayed complications found swelling in 42.3 percent, lumps or nodules in 25.0 percent and xanthelasma-like reactions in 17.3 percent; 98 percent of the patients were female, average age 48.3, and HA was the product in 71.2 percent, with poly-L-lactic acid and calcium hydroxylapatite each in 7.7 percent [2].

A case report described orbital compartment syndrome from retrobulbar haemorrhage after tear trough filler, treated surgically without lasting visual compromise, and was presented as the first such report [5]. A separate 2024 case report series covers injection-related visual compromise more broadly [25]. Wikipedia describes vascular occlusion leading to blindness as rare, with vision loss usually permanent [13], and the FDA lists unintentional injection into a blood vessel as the most concerning filler risk, advising immediate care for vision changes or unusual pain [14].

In the United States the FDA regulates fillers as medical devices that a licensed provider injects. Its consumer page lists approved indications such as wrinkles and folds, lip and cheek augmentation and the back of the hand, and does not list the under-eye area; it also states that no filler is approved for over-the-counter use, warns about counterfeit products and advises against self-injection and buying filler online [14]. Wikipedia reports that in the UK and European Economic Area fillers need a CE mark covering manufacturing standards, and that over 140 fillers are on the European market against six approved in the US [13].

Human research includes systematic reviews of techniques and of delayed complications [3][2], retrospective cohorts [4][7], a consecutive case series [8], clinical trials of HA, composite and cell-based products [24][19][20][21] and a case report of an orbital complication [5]. Registered trials include a platelet-rich fibrin study [9], a two-filler pilot [10] and the RHA Redensity Eye versus no-treatment study [11]. Analyses of public search interest, including a Google Trends study of 20 cosmetic procedures, show tear trough filler interest changing by more than 50 percent within single weeks [6][26].

A looksmax.org user reported having both tear trough and jaw filler in one session at a total cost of about 450 dollars from a plastic surgeon. The poster described little downtime beyond swelling and said the change was noticeable in person but hard to capture in photographs; replies were mostly sceptical or asked for photos and prices [12].

Other threads treat the under-eye as a structural question. One poster with a hereditary-looking hollow asks whether the problem sits at bone level, and another says fat placed in the trough might sag with age without bone support [17]. A further thread links to a user's account of resolving the under-eye area through a combination of methods found on the forum[16].

timeline.event: Karl Ferdinand von Graefe coins the term blepharoplasty for eyelid repair [15].
Dermal fillers become widely used for facial appearance [13].
A pilot of two HA fillers for the lower eyelid is registered (NCT00852241) [10].
A consecutive series of 198 eyes reports HA filler as an alternative to lower eyelid surgery [8].
A multicentre safety evaluation of a semi-cross-linked HA filler for tear trough rejuvenation is published [24].
The RHA Redensity Eye versus no-treatment study for infraorbital hollows starts (NCT04577898) [11].
Systematic reviews of HA tear trough techniques and of delayed complications are published [3][2].
A series of 1,452 tear trough applications describes a three-point tangent cannula technique [7].
The first reported orbital compartment syndrome after tear trough filler is published [5].

lore.intro: Under-eye filler appears on looksmax.org mainly as personal reports and questions about whether a hollow is fixable, with fat grafting and filler compared and the eye area treated as a high-impact feature [12][16][17].

claims.claim: Tear trough filler gives a noticeable improvement without looking plastic and with little downtime
claims.believers: A poster who had the procedure says small corrections are immediately noticeable in person without a plastic look, with swelling as the only downtime [12].
claims.experts: A retrospective review found swelling in over half of patients after infraorbital HA filler without triamcinolone [4], and a case series reported satisfaction over about five months of follow-up [8].

claims.claim: Tear trough filler is low risk
claims.believers: The same poster describes only swelling and a quick recovery [12].
claims.experts: Reviews list delayed swelling, nodules and discoloration [2], a case report documents orbital compartment syndrome [5], and the FDA lists vascular occlusion and blindness as rare but serious filler risks [14].

claims.claim: A hollow with a bony cause will not hold filler or fat well
claims.believers: Posters ask whether a deep trough is a bone-level problem and suggest tissue placed there may sag later without bone support [17].
claims.experts: Reviews describe filler as camouflaging the hollow by volume [1]; none of the reviewed studies compared outcomes by underlying bony structure.

claims.claim: Fat grafting is better than filler for the tear trough
claims.believers: A thread weighs filler against fat grafting for the tear trough, with a poster presenting a combination of methods that they say resolved their under-eye area [16].
claims.experts: Wikipedia notes autologous fat transfer as a way to restore periorbital volume in lower eyelid surgery [15], while the filler literature is mainly retrospective [3]; no trial compares fat and HA directly in the studies reviewed.

claims.claim: Cannula injection is safer than needle injection
claims.believers: A large series describes a cannula technique built on tailored linear paths for the tear trough [7].
claims.experts: A systematic review found no significant difference in aesthetic results and no evidence-based standard between needle and cannula, and it was aiming to establish a preference to prevent adverse events [3].

claims.claim: Filler is a non-surgical substitute for lower eyelid surgery
claims.believers: A published series evaluated HA filler specifically as an alternative to lower eyelid surgery [8].
claims.experts: Blepharoplasty reviews describe different anatomical indications, such as skin laxity needing a skin approach, and state that fat repositioning or transfer is part of surgery [18][15].
